answer.rationale: Causal reasoning first: the write-path p99 began climbing 90 minutes ago and a release shipped 2 hours ago. That ~30-minute offset is consistent with a bad build whose effect emerges under load, so the release is the leading hypothesis. The competing hypothesis is pure load (settlement peak, heavy writes), which the release timing does not explain away. Rollback is the only candidate that directly removes the suspected cause; the others treat symptoms. Regional failover (memory_b2) is wrong here because a bad build is present in every region and failover moves the defect rather than removing it, while adding failover risk to in-flight writes. Add capacity (memory_b3) worked pre-emptively before a known peak, not as a 90-minute mitigation, and provisioning lead time likely exceeds the incident window. Circuit breakers (memory_b4) fit a failing external dependency, and nothing here indicates a partner fault; opening a breaker on the write path would shed exactly the customer writes we are told not to lose. Read-replica routing (memory_b5) relieved a read-heavy primary; the current pressure is write-side, so relief would be marginal at best, though it is the sensible fallback if rollback is disconfirmed. I want to verify memory_b1 because it is the single memory I am leaning hardest on, and the consolidated summary is compressed to a happy ending: I need the source record to check whether the prior build was actually verified stable, whether the rollback ran under peak write load or during a quiet window, and whether schema or data migrations were involved. If that release carried a forward migration, rolling back is not symmetric and could corrupt or drop settlement writes, which would invert the recommendation. I want memory_b6 because it tells me whether canary gating was in force for today's release: if the staged gate exists and passed, the release is less likely the cause and the load hypothesis gains weight; if gating was bypassed for this ship, the release hypothesis strengthens considerably. Note a base-rate problem across this entire inherited set: all six memories record successes and none record an intervention that failed or made things worse. That is survivorship-shaped and means the stored confidence in each playbook is probably inflated; I am discounting accordingly rather than treating these as validated priors. Hence scale is a small guarded rollback: revert a limited cohort of write traffic to the prior build with an explicit abort trigger and write-drain protection, and watch p99 for a clear signal before going wider. This keeps customer writes intact if the release is innocent and buys evidence rather than spending the one intervention on a guess. Downstream value risk is real and flagged: whatever I do today gets consolidated into memory as another clean success story, and a rollback that coincides with the settlement peak passing on its own would write a false causal lesson into the record for the next agent. I will record the outcome with the load confound stated explicitly, and note the disconfirming case if latency does not recover, so the memory carries its own uncertainty forward.
